# John contacts of a balanced moment body retain an integer dual term

This note proves attainment and uniqueness facts for the **original-source** support duals of a balanced moment body, combines them using actual John contact equations, and derives a joint hinge bound. It also gives an exact obstruction to cancelling their integer coefficients. The resulting identities concern source moments and hinge integrals; no OC cap-mass guarantee or universal choice of the mass parameter is asserted.

## 1. Definitions and strict-mass support-dual attainment

Let `P` be a finite nonempty subset of `Z^n`, let each `K_z` be a positive-volume compact convex body in `R^d`, where `d>=1`, and suppose their lifted convex hull has these actual integer fibers. Let

\[
\mu=\sum_{z\in P}\delta_z\otimes 1_{K_z}\,dx,
\qquad w_z=|K_z|,
\]

and fix `j in P`. The same statements work with a common positive constant `c` multiplying `dx`, provided every fiber weight is then defined as `w_z=mu({z} x K_z)=c|K_z|`. Put

\[
T=\max\left\{\int f\,d\mu:0\le f\le1,\quad
\int(z-j)f\,d\mu=0\right\}.
\]

For `0<t<T` define the compact convex moment body

\[
\mathcal M_t(j)=\left\{\frac1t\int xf\,d\mu:
0\le f\le1,\quad\int f\,d\mu=t,\quad
\int(z-j)f\,d\mu=0\right\}.
\]

The elementary compactness and positive-inradius proofs are in `candidate b4c3b9c6a52059d2` and `candidate cf94bd7190201a57`. In particular `M_t(j)` is a full-dimensional convex body contained in `K_j`.

**Lemma 1.** For every nonzero `u in R^d`, the dual formula

\[
t h_{\mathcal M_t(j)}(u)
=\min_{a\in\mathbb R^n,b\in\mathbb R}
\left[tb+\int(u\cdot x+a\cdot(z-j)-b)_+\,d\mu\right]
\tag{1}
\]

has an attained minimum. A minimizing pair can be chosen so that its closed cap

\[
H_u=\{u\cdot x+a\cdot(z-j)-b\ge0\}
\]

has mass exactly `t` and integer centroid `j`. The maximizing dominated source in direction `u` is unique up to `mu`-null sets and is `1_(H_u) mu`.

**Proof.** Let `F` be the minimal face of `conv(P)` containing `j`, and put `P_F=P intersect F`, `V=span(F-j)`. Then `j` belongs to the relative interior of `F`. Every nonnegative source with base mean `j` is supported on `P_F`: a functional exposing `F` is zero there and strictly negative on every other base point, and its source integral must be zero.

There are positive numbers `p_z`, for **all** `z in P_F`, with sum one and `sum p_z(z-j)=0`. Indeed, for each `z`, a sufficiently short displacement from `j` in direction `j-z` remains in `F`; its convex representation, combined with a positive weight on `z`, represents `j`. Averaging these finitely many representations gives the asserted strictly positive coefficients. Choose `s<t` so small that `e_z=s p_z<w_z`. Take an attained maximum balanced mass vector `m_z^T` of total `T` and mix it with `e` to obtain total `t`:

\[
m_z^0=\frac{T-t}{T-s}e_z+\frac{t-s}{T-s}m_z^T.
\]

Then `0<m_z^0<w_z` on every `z in P_F`. The source `f_0=m_z^0/w_z` constant on each such fiber is balanced, has mass `t`, and satisfies `delta<=f_0<=1-delta` for one `delta>0`.

Restrict `a` to `V` and temporarily integrate only over `P_F`. Writing `q=a.(z-j)-b`, the dual objective satisfies

\[
tb+\int(u\cdot x+q)_+\,d\mu_F
=\int[(u\cdot x+q)_+-f_0q],d\mu_F
\ge\delta\int|q|\,d\mu_F-\int|u\cdot x|\,d\mu_F.
\tag{2}
\]

The function `sum_(P_F) w_z |a.(z-j)-b|` is a norm on `V x R`: its kernel has `b=0` from the base `j`, and then `a=0` because the base differences span `V`. Thus the continuous objective is coercive on this finite-dimensional space and attains a minimum.

Since `u!=0` and every fiber has full dimension `d`, its cap boundary has zero `mu_F` mass. Differentiating the objective with respect to `b` and to `a in V` therefore gives, at its minimum, mass `t` and zero base moment. This differentiation follows directly from dominated convergence for the positive part; the finite bounded support bounds all parameter derivatives. Its cap source is consequently feasible in the primal problem. The weak-duality inequality

\[
(u\cdot x+q)f\le(u\cdot x+q)_+
\]

shows that the cap's attained moment equals the dual minimum and the primal support maximum. Finally add to `a` a sufficiently large positive multiple of a functional zero on `F-j` and negative at every other base. Bounded fibers and finiteness of `P` then make the cap strictly empty outside `P_F`, without changing any retained trace. This realizes (1) on the original source.

For uniqueness, any other maximizing feasible density `f` has

\[
\int (u\cdot x+q)(1_{H_u}-f)\,d\mu=0.
\]

The integrand is nonnegative, and its coefficient is nonzero almost everywhere. It follows that `f=1_(H_u)` almost everywhere. This proves the lemma. In particular every exposed face of `M_t(j)` is a singleton. The pair `(a,b)` need not itself be unique. ∎

## 2. Finite John contacts and their actual source witnesses

Let `E=c+A B_d` be a maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid of `M_t(j)`, where `A` is symmetric positive definite. Existence follows by compactness of bounded ellipsoid centers and shape matrices, continuity of determinant, and the positive inball of `M_t(j)`. Normalize continuous coordinates by `xi=A^(-1)(x-c)`; the normalized body contains the unit ball as a maximum-volume inscribed ellipsoid.

There are unit contact normals `v_i` and positive weights `lambda_i`, with at most `d+d(d+1)/2` nonzero terms, satisfying

\[
\sum_i\lambda_i v_i=0,\qquad
\sum_i\lambda_i v_i v_i^T=I_d,
\qquad \sum_i\lambda_i=d.
\tag{3}
\]

For completeness, these equations follow by finite-dimensional separation. For the normalized body let `V_c={v:|v|=1,h(v)=1}`. The cone generated by `(v,vv^T)`, `v in V_c`, is closed: each generator has second-component trace one, so a bounded convergent sequence in the cone has bounded total coefficient and convergent subsequences of the associated probability averages. If `(0,I)` were outside the cone, separation would give a translation vector `p` and symmetric matrix `B` with `tr(B)>0` and `p.v+v^T Bv<=0` on all contacts. Replace `B` by `B-epsilon I` for small `epsilon>0`; the trace remains positive and the displayed inequality becomes uniformly strict. The ellipsoid with center `epsilon' p` and shape `I+epsilon' B` then remains inside the body for all sufficiently small `epsilon'>0`: its support has negative first derivative uniformly near the compact contact set, while directions outside a fixed neighborhood have a positive support gap. Its volume increases because `tr(B)>0`, a contradiction. Conic Caratheodory, or elementary elimination of a linear dependence among more than `d+d(d+1)/2` generators, gives (3).

In the original coordinates put `u_i=A^(-1)v_i`. Then

\[
h_{\mathcal M_t}(u_i)=u_i\cdot c+1,\qquad
\sum_i\lambda_i u_i=0.
\]

Apply Lemma 1 to each **same original-source** direction `u_i`, obtaining actual caps

\[
H_i=\{L_i\ge0\},\quad
L_i(z,x)=u_i\cdot x+a_i\cdot(z-j)-b_i,
\quad \Psi_i=\int(L_i)_+\,d\mu.
\]

They satisfy

\[
\mu(H_i)=t,\qquad\int_{H_i}(z-j)\,d\mu=0,
\qquad\frac1t\int_{H_i}x\,d\mu=c+A v_i.
\tag{4}
\]

The last assertion is stronger than just a support-value identity. The ellipsoid contact point `c+A v_i` lies in `M_t` and attains its support in direction `u_i`. Lemma 1 makes that support point unique, so it equals the cap source's centroid.

Thus

\[
\sigma=\frac1d\sum_i\lambda_i\mu|_{H_i}
\tag{5}
\]

is a dominated source of mass `t`, base centroid `j`, and continuous centroid exactly `c`. Moreover its constituent source centroids have covariance `A^2/d` under the weights `lambda_i/d`. These assertions use actual caps from the original measure, rather than independently chosen artificial directional measures.

## 3. The surviving integer term and a joint bound

Set

\[
\bar a=\sum_i\lambda_i a_i,
\qquad B=\sum_i\lambda_i b_i.
\]

The exact support-dual values and (3) give

\[
\boxed{\ \sum_i\lambda_i\Psi_i=t(d-B).\ }
\tag{6}
\]

Positive-part subadditivity retains the integer aggregate:

\[
\boxed{\ t(d-B)\ge
\int\bigl(\bar a\cdot(z-j)-B\bigr)_+\,d\mu.\ }
\tag{7}
\]

Indeed `sum lambda_i L_i=bar a.(z-j)-B`; the continuous coefficients cancel and the integer coefficients generally do not. Testing the last integrand on any attained balanced source of mass `T` gives the lower bound `-BT`. Combining it with (7) yields

\[
B\ge-\frac{dt}{T-t},\qquad
\boxed{\ \sum_i\lambda_i\Psi_i\le\frac{dtT}{T-t}.\ }
\tag{8}
\]

There is no sign restriction on `B` needed in this argument: for every `0<=f_T<=1`, the pointwise inequality `q_+>=q f_T` is valid for both signs of `q`. The bound depends on the maximum **balanced** mass `T`, not on an integral replacing the integer fibers. It is a hinge bound with the continuous John normalization, not a cap-mass lower bound at `c`.

## 4. A regular exact example where the integer normals cannot cancel

Use the actual three-interval body from `candidate 5939c45de14c2bb5`:

\[
K_{-1}=[-21/80,-13/80],\quad
K_0=[-1/2,1/2],\quad
K_1=[-59/80,5/16].
\]

Its total mass is `43/20`, its unique weighted integer centerpoint is `j=0`, its capacity is `D_0=11/10`, and `T=6/5`. At the prescribed strictly feasible mass `t=D_0/2=11/20`, its moment body and John ellipsoid coincide with the interval

\[
\mathcal M_t(0)=[-163/440,619/2640],\qquad
c=-359/5280,\qquad R=1597/5280.
\]

The two raw directions `+1,-1` have the following exact dual pairs:

\[
(a_+,b_+)=(-19/80,1/30),\qquad
(a_-,b_-)=(-39/80,3/20).
\tag{9}
\]

For the positive direction the retained masses at `-1,0,1` are `(1/24,7/15,1/24)`. For the negative direction they are `(1/10,7/20,1/10)`. Each triple has mass `11/20` and base mean zero. Their centroids are exactly the two displayed interval endpoints, so Lemma 1 or direct threshold exchange proves dual optimality.

Both dual pairs are unique. Near the positive pair all three fibers are cut properly, and the Hessian in `(a,-b)` is `sum (z,1)(z,1)^T`, namely `diag(2,3)`. Near the negative pair only fibers `0,1` are cut properly, giving the positive-definite matrix `[[1,1],[1,2]]`; the other fiber is strictly full. These are genuine neighborhoods of transverse cuts. Thus both convex dual objectives are locally strictly convex at their minima, which excludes a distinct global minimum (the connecting segment would contradict local strict convexity).

After transforming `x=c+R xi`, the John normals are `+1,-1` in `xi`, with weights `lambda_+=lambda_-=1/2`. The integer coefficients become `a_+/R,a_-/R`, and therefore

\[
\bar a=\frac{a_++a_-}{2R}=-\frac{1914}{1597}\ne0.
\tag{10}
\]

No positive weighting of these two source normals can cancel the full ambient normal: continuous cancellation forces equal weights, while their integer sum is nonzero. No alternative minimizing tilt repairs it because the two pairs in (9) are unique. In this normalization,

\[
B=\frac{484}{1597},\qquad
\sum_i\lambda_i\Psi_i=\frac{12243}{31940},\qquad
\int(\bar a z-B)_+\,d\mu=\frac{143}{1597},
\]

which checks (6)--(8) explicitly. The upper bound in (8) is `66/65`.

The actual John center fails the OC budget at this fixed mass: the oblique closed cap

\[
x\le c-\frac{707}{1056}z
\]

has mass `2809/5280`, strictly below `M/4=2838/5280`. This cap's integer first moment is `-1/10`, unlike the balanced source-dual caps. Thus even the contact direction's balanced source tilt does not control all other ambient tilts. This is precisely the distinction kept in (7).

The counterexample does **not** rule out optimizing `t`: the source note explicitly finds smaller masses whose centers succeed in this same body.

## 5. Basic calibration and remaining scope

For a uniform interval source of total mass `M` on a unit interval (or identical fibers with overall base centroid `j`),

\[
\mathcal M_t(j)=[t/(2M),1-t/(2M)],
\quad c=1/2,\quad R=(M-t)/(2M).
\]

The two John-normalized support hinges both equal `t^2/(M-t)`. Therefore (8), with `d=1,T=M`, is asymptotically sharp as `t/M` tends to one: the ratio of its two sides tends to one. The bound cannot be replaced by `sum lambda_i Psi_i<=t` for all `t`, since the displayed value exceeds `t` when `t>M/2`.

The new conclusions are the strict-mass dual attainment, unique cap support sources at every direction, their exact John contact moments, and the joint inequality (7)--(8). The nonzero integer coefficient (10) is an exact obstruction to obtaining an ambient positive-normal circuit by simply applying John balance. No assertion that John contacts alone imply depth, or that some mass parameter must achieve OC, is used or proved.

## 6. Maximizing ellipsoid volume over the mass parameter has a boundary supremum

Let `J(t)` be the volume of a largest inscribed ellipsoid of `M_t(j)`, and `J_K` the corresponding volume for `K_j`. Then

\[
0<s<t<T\implies \mathcal M_t(j)\subset\mathcal M_s(j),
\qquad \lim_{t\downarrow0}J(t)=J_K,
\qquad J(t)<J_K\quad(t>0).
\tag{11}
\]

Consequently maximizing this ellipsoid-volume objective over `0<t<T` has no attained maximum. Its supremum is the original fiber's John volume at the excluded endpoint `t=0`. This statement concerns **volume optimization**; optimizing actual halfspace depth along the resulting centers is a different objective.

For the nesting, replace a feasible mass-`t` density by `(s/t)f`, which leaves its centroid unchanged. For convergence, let `w=mu({j} x K_j)` and `theta=(s/w)^(1/d)` for `s<w`. For each `p in K_j`, the homothetic body `(1-theta)p+theta K_j` has source mass `s` and centroid `(1-theta)p+theta g_(K_j)`. Thus

\[
(1-\theta)K_j+\theta g_{K_j}\subset\mathcal M_s(j)\subset K_j.
\]

This proves Hausdorff convergence and
`(1-theta)^d J_K <= J(s) <= J_K`.

It remains to verify the strict assertion, rather than infer it from proper inclusion alone. In fact `M_t(j) subset int K_j` for every positive feasible `t`. Suppose a represented centroid `(j,x)` had `x in boundary K_j`. As in Lemma 1, reduce to the minimal face `F` of `conv(P)` containing `j`. The convex hull `C_F` of the fibers over `P_F` has relative dimension `dim(F)+d`, and `(j,x)` is on its relative boundary: relative interior would give a continuous ball in the `j` fiber. A supporting affine functional at this point has a nonzero continuous component. Otherwise its base component would support `F` at its relative-interior point `j`, forcing the whole functional to be zero in the relative ambient space. The nonnegative support deficit of this functional has integral zero under the represented source, because its centroid is the contact point. That source must therefore be supported on the supporting hyperplane. The nonzero continuous component makes the hyperplane have zero `mu` mass on every fiber, a contradiction to `t>0`.

Since `M_t(j)` is compact and lies inside `int K_j`, a sufficiently small dilation about any point in `M_t(j)` remains inside `K_j`. Dilating its inscribed ellipsoid at the same time gives an ellipsoid in `K_j` with strictly larger volume than `J(t)`. This proves strictness in (11).
